content: Dental caries continues to be a significant public health issue in most industrialized nations, affecting between 60% and 90% of school-aged children and the majority of adults. Fluoridated milk has been proposed as a potentially cost-effective method for delivering fluoride to prevent dental caries. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of fluoridated milk in reducing dental caries at the community level. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to November 2014. Additional searches were conducted in the U.S. National Institutes of Health Trials Register and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform to identify ongoing trials. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date during the search process. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared fluoridated milk with non-fluoridated milk, with an intervention and follow-up period of at least two years. Two independent reviewers assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and extracted relevant data using standard Cochrane methodological procedures. Only one unpublished RCT met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 180 children, aged three years at the start of the trial, who attended nursery schools in an area with a high prevalence of dental caries and low fluoride levels in drinking water. Data from 166 participants were analyzed. The study was determined to have a high risk of bias. After three years, the results showed a reduction in dental caries in both primary and permanent teeth. For primary teeth, the mean difference (MD) in the decayed, missing, and filled teeth index (dmft) was −1.14 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −1.86 to −0.42), representing a substantial reduction equivalent to a prevented fraction of 31%. For permanent teeth, the MD in the DMFT index was −0.13 (95% CI: −0.24 to −0.02), but the absolute effect size was small due to the low baseline level of disease in permanent teeth. The study did not report on other outcomes of interest, such as adverse events, dental pain, antibiotic use, or the need for general anesthesia due to dental procedures. The authors concluded that there is low-quality evidence suggesting that fluoridated milk may be beneficial in reducing dental caries in primary teeth among schoolchildren. However, the evidence is limited by the small size of the included study, its high risk of bias, and the lack of information on potential harms associated with the intervention. Further high-quality RCTs are needed to provide more definitive conclusions regarding the effectiveness and safety of milk fluoridation.
